extracted.intended_audience: arts teachers, arts administrators, arts educators, and others seeking funding for school arts programs
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step practical guidance for developing and submitting grant proposals for school arts programs, including needs assessment, budget development, funder targeting, and proposal formatting and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Needs assessment (Statement of Problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The needs assessment--basically, why there is a need for what it is you want to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer who needs help; what they cannot now do; what they could accomplish with help; what sort of help is needed; how long it will take; where the work will be done; who will do it; what it will cost; who will be interested and who will benefit. Show awareness of similar activities elsewhere to avoid duplication and to justify ripple effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The rationale / Introduction (Who you are and why you should do it)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale--who you are and why you are the group or person to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish why you or your group should be the ones to carry out the project: what the situation should be like, why you can bring it about, who else is doing similar projects, how your project ties in with theirs, what value your specific project adds, why here, why now, why you. Include endorsements, press quotes, letters of support to establish credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives (Goals and expected results)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective--your goal; what it is you want to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be as specific and as brief as possible. Objectives are the specific results you expect from your program — avoid vague statements and pick a particular target you believe you can meet. Check that objectives align with the needs assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods (How you will do it)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method--how you will go about doing it. (This should be concise, but very specific in terms of means to your ends.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe exactly what you'll be doing, who will do it, and when. Include a timetable for each phase. Demonstrate familiarity with alternative methods and explain why yours are better. Pare down to a bald, accurate account that clearly meets objectives. Build in time for delays and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget (Heart of the proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The budget--what it will cost. A realistic budget is extremely important because it shows you have thought out and carefully planned what you are going to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic—budgets that are too skimpy or inflated can break a proposal. Divide costs under Contributed Funds and Requested Funds; show major in-kind contributions and dollar equivalents. Include wages/salaries, benefits, fees, rentals, travel, telephone, postage, printing, insurance, etc. Recheck and refine figures; prepare Plans A/B/C (ideal, sensible, minimum). Get local price quotes, include publication and dissemination costs, and have someone with accounting knowledge check layout/format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel and facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The personnel and facilities involved--who will be the people on your staff (existing and hired), where it will take place, and what the time period will be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify percentage of staff time, rental costs, and ensure details dovetail with the budget. For sizable requests, include resumes/CVs of project director and key staff as appendices. Indicate likelihood of future support and, if possible, provide letters of commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and dissemination of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation and dissemination of the results--how will you assess the effectiveness of your project and enable others to share your experiences and results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail how you will measure success (monitoring, reappraisal, evaluation sheets, internal/external reviewers), how you will report to sponsors, and how you will disseminate results (publications, filmstrips, media). Include evaluation/dissemination costs in the budget. Proofs of success may include increased support or replication requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract / Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract, or summary of all the above; essentially this is the last element you write, but it will be the first element your recipient reads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the summary last but ensure it serves as a clear, concise first page. Many funders prescreen on the basis of the summary; include it in the cover letter or at the start of the application form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight Elements of a Good Proposal (format checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: All proposals have the same main constituents: Summary, Introduction, Statement of Problem (Needs Assessment), Objectives, Methods, Evaluation, Future and Additional Funding, Budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this structure as appropriate for the funder; keep each section short and succinct; put detailed material into appendices. The booklet lists specific expectations for each element (see individual elements above).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show ripple effect and non-duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that your project will have 'ripple effect' and that you are not duplicating work being done by somebody else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the needs assessment show awareness of similar activities elsewhere and how your project adds value. Funders want assurance that their investment benefits more than the immediate participants and that publicity/dissemination will credit the sponsor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate targeting of funding source (Four Rules of Thumb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose funding sources appropriate to the cost and scope of the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four rules of thumb from the booklet: (1) For sums of $200-750, seek help from local businesses and corporations. (2) $500 is the breakpoint above which you should consider seeking help outside your local community. (3) For sums of $750-2,500, seek help from foundations. (4) For sums of $2,500 upward, seek help from state (and federal) agencies and foundations. Adapt your approach (letter, outline, in-person) to the type of funder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow funder-specific guidelines and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere specifically to funder requests for form and content, and observe strict deadlines (especially for federal agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study program guides and proposal guidelines carefully. Use agency contacts (program officers) for advice; submit abstracts first where recommended; incorporate their recommendations before preparing a full proposal. Failure to meet form or deadline can be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach method tailored to funder type
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust approach and materials depending on whether you target foundations, corporations, small businesses, or government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations: research (Foundation Center, catalogs), follow written guidelines, submit proposals per their format. Corporations: letter of inquiry often preferred; identify director of corporate giving or public relations officer. Small businesses: one-to-one approach with brief memo and pictures; emphasize local publicity potential. For federal funds use Federal Register/Catalog of Federal Domestic Assistance and contact program staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match or in-kind expectations (e.g., NEA matching requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of matching fund expectations or in-kind requirements from certain funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: National Endowment for the Arts programs expect preparation to match funds requested with equivalent funds or in-kind support. Show other sources or in-kind contributions to strengthen the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and supporting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Include supporting materials (resumes/CVs, letters of support, press clippings, detailed budgets, graphs/charts) as appendices rather than in the main text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the main proposal concise and put detailed documentation in appendices so readers can find vital information quickly if they want to learn more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, concision and human voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal should be concise, simple, and clearly expressed and appear to have been written by a human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon, write simply, hold the reader's attention, keep sections short, and use appendices for detail. Have someone unfamiliar read your proposal to check clarity and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget: include underestimated/overlooked items
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure to include commonly overlooked costs and to document how estimates were compiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't forget postage, telephone, editorial costs, publication and mailing costs, equipment rental fees, per diems, inflation/merit increases. Get local price estimates and check costs of services (camera operator, printing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale projects and prepare contingency plans (Plans A/B/C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess different funding scenarios: ideal (A), sensible (B), and minimum (C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what can be accomplished at each funding level and identify possible in-kind contributions or cost reductions so you can scale the project sensibly if you receive less than ideal funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allies, advisory councils and community contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Find an ally and develop local contacts, advisory councils, or cosponsors to strengthen proposals and access local resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk ideas over with friends or stakeholders, enlist parents, administrators, local merchants, chambers of commerce, service clubs, and form advisory councils to both gain support and generate initial donations or in-kind help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research funders and use grantsmanship resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do homework using resources like the Federal Register, Catalog of Federal Domestic Assistance, Foundation Center, Mitchell Guide, and local Educational Improvement Centers (EICs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indexes and past grant descriptions to identify funders likely to support your subject area. Put your name on agency mailing lists and consult grantsmanship staff for targeted advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make personal contact and follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: Make telephone or in-person contact with funders and follow up on mailed inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call program contacts with an abstract/summary, ask for program guides, put your name on mailing lists, and follow up by phone if you don't hear back within a week. Personal contact can improve chances and clarify expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Define what will constitute proof of success and include methods for collecting that proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs of success may include increased financial support, requests from other groups to use your model, media coverage, or documented outcomes. Plan how you will gather publicity and evidence for sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score Your Own Proposal — checklist items (12 evaluation items)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 12-item self-scoring checklist to evaluate proposal effectiveness using a 0–5 scale for each item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items to score: (1) The project reflects distinctly identified needs; (2) Objectives are well defined and clearly stated; (3) Methods of achieving objectives are detailed and appropriate; (4) The facilities and equipment are sufficient and time frame practical; (5) Staff members proposed have requisite skills and knowledge; (6) The budget is carefully thought out and contains nothing extraneous; (7) Anticipated costs are reasonable in relation to anticipated results; (8) The applicant shows responsibility and competence in accounting and record-keeping; (9) Direction, roles of project personnel and responsibility for decision making are clearly defined; (10) There are provisions for adequate evaluation of the project's effectiveness; (11) Plans for dissemination are well researched and complete; (12) The proposal is concise, simple and clearly expressed, and appears to have been written by a human being. Use combined/average score to decide next steps (0-1 rethink, 2-3 rewrite, 4 sharpen details, 5 mail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and follow-up etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: How to present brief proposals, letters, and follow-up actions depending on funder and project size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small local funders prepare a one-page description and present in person if possible; follow up by phone; invite sponsors to events. For larger funders follow formal guidelines, include letters of support, and be prompt and specific in responding to requests for additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping and accountability for sponsors
rubrics_metrics.description: Show capability for responsible accounting and reporting to sponsors about how funds were spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include in the proposal how you will track expenditures, provide regular reports to sponsors, and maintain records; funders want assurance of accountability for future funding prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability and persistence (rewriting & re-targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to rewrite and resubmit proposals to different funders; use rejections as practice and adapt proposals to new audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If refused, revise and target to other potential sponsors (local merchants, civic groups, other foundations); tailor format and content to each prospective source.
